name: Calcium supplements
short: Heart attack: 1 trial meta-analysis found more (calcium alone), a later one no significant rise; review: 10-20% more. More kidney stones (review; vitamin D trial, postmenopausal women); gut problems.
text: On heart and blood vessel events the trial evidence is two-sided. A 2010 meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials of calcium supplements given without vitamin D found more myocardial infarctions (heart attacks) with calcium, both in patient-level data from 5 trials (8,151 participants; hazard ratio 1.31) and in trial-level data from 11 trials (11,921 participants; relative risk 1.27), with non-significant rises in stroke and death. In contrast, a 2023 meta-analysis of 11 placebo-controlled trials found that calcium alone (8,634 participants) or with vitamin D (46,804 participants) was not significantly associated with heart attack, coronary heart disease death, stroke or death from any cause. A 2025 review states that meta-analyses of trial adverse events suggest a 10-20% increase in heart attack risk and that calcium supplements commonly cause gastrointestinal side effects, sometimes serious, and increase the risk of kidney stones. In the Women's Health Initiative trial in 36,282 postmenopausal women, calcium plus vitamin D increased kidney stones (hazard ratio 1.17). In a 5-year trial of calcium carbonate in 1,460 women over 70, constipation was the only adverse event that increased (13.4% versus 9.1% with placebo), and an analysis of seven trials found self-reported gastrointestinal adverse events more common with calcium (14.1% versus 10.0%), with adjudicated gastrointestinal hospital admissions of 6.8% versus 3.6% in one study; however, a small 8-week crossover study in 27 healthy women found no change in stool frequency or form with calcium carbonate or calcium phosphate. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
